ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All study procedures were approved by the institutional review board at Dartmouth College.
Approval was obtained from the ethics committee of Dartmouth College.
The procedures used in this study adhere to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were recruited from introductory psychology and neuroscience courses and received course credit for their participation.
Prior to the experiment, they provided written informed consent.
Data from one subject had to be excluded from the final analyses because they only completed five trials of the experiment.

For the first four subjects, there were technical issues with the loudspeakers during the first block of the experiment; thus, to avoid losing data, we added an additional learning block for these participants during data collection.
After exclusion, data from 33 participants were retained for the main analyses.

One of the sounds contained a short 25ms gap (the target), and the other did not, and participants were tasked to detect the sound with the gap and report which side this target tone came from (left vs. right) by pressing the left or down-key on a keyboard, respectively.

To reduce the influence of differences in perceived loudness between the three pitches, before beginning the experiment, participants completed a sound thresholding task to adjust the pitch intensities based on perceived loudness for each subject.
Specifically, participants were asked to compare the loudness of two sounds, hearing them in succession and incrementally adjusting the first sound to match the second sound's perceived loudness.
Following the experiment, participants completed a post-experiment questionnaire assessing awareness of the statistical structure and strategies used.

Most participants did not report attending to a specific sound, and when asked to identify the most frequent target sound, performance was roughly at chance (with the exception of the high-pitch sound, which participants were more likely to select regardless of assignment, suggesting some influence of bottom-up salience).

Mean RTs were under a second (M = 712.67, SD = 128.23), and as can be seen in Figure 2B, participants were fastest for the valid condition (M = 698.03, SD = 131.00), followed by the neutral condition (M = 718.79, SD = 127.09) and finally the invalid condition (M = 737.09, SD = 143.47).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were recruited from introductory psychology and neuroscience courses and received course credit for their participation. Prior to the experiment, they provided written informed consent. All study procedures were approved by the institutional review board at Dartmouth College. Sample size was determined based on a pilot experiment (N = 29) that used an identical task but without the thresholding procedure, which yielded an effect size of d ≈ 0.30. We considered effect sizes in the range of d = 0.20-0.50 to be theoretically meaningful for this paradigm and anticipated that equating perceived loudness across sounds via the thresholding procedure would increase the effect size toward a medium effect (d ≈ 0.50), which requires N = 34 to achieve 80% power (α = 0.05) in a paired t-test. Accordingly, we aimed to collect approximately 34 participants for Experiments 1 and 2.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 146 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (146). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

text.text: Listeners navigate complex acoustic environments by selectively attending to relevant sounds amid competing noise.

This capacity is classically attributed to top-down goals and bottom-up salience, but recent work implicates a third influence: selection history, whereby incidental exposure to statistical regularities shapes attentional prioritization.
We investigated how incidental experience of selecting specific acoustic features influences attentional prioritization across different levels of auditory processing.
Participants listened to two concurrently presented sounds to detect a target that contained a brief temporal gap.
Unbeknownst to the participants, during a learning phase, one sound was more likely to contain the target gap; in a subsequent testing phase all sounds were equally likely to be the target.
Experiment 1 used pure tones of varying pitches, and Experiment 2 used instrument chords (piano, trumpet, guitar).

Across both experiments, participants responded faster to high-probability targets during learning, indicating facilitated attentional selection based on the statistical regularities across different levels of acoustic representations.

This response time advantage persisted robustly throughout the unbiased testing phase for Experiment 1, but less so for Experiment 2, possibly suggesting that the persistence of experience-driven auditory attention may depend on the complexity of the learned feature.
Overall, our findings parallel selection-history effects observed in vision, providing evidence that similar influences of incidental experience on attentional priors exist across sensory modalities.

In many situations, we are confronted with multiple auditory inputs at once, requiring us to select which sounds are most relevant for ongoing behavior: We might need to detect a bike bell amidst traffic noise, pick out our phone notification in a loud café, or notice a baby crying while music is playing.
How does the auditory system identify and prioritize behaviorally relevant sounds amidst competing acoustic inputs?

Classic work on auditory attention has focused on explicit, top-down influences of attention, where observers are tasked to selectively attend to one auditory stream over another (e.g., left vs. right ear, female vs. male voice, etc.), demonstrating that top-down, intentional selection can enhance processing of attended relative to unattended input (Hansen & Hillyard, 1980; Woldorff et al., 1993; Degerman et al., 2006; Broadbent, 1957).

However, emerging evidence indicates that another source influences perceptual selection: incidental experience with frequently encountered targets, often termed selection history (Awh et al., 2012).

Even without explicit instructions, people are faster in identifying targets that are more frequently associated with a particular location (Addleman et al., 2019; Geng & Behrmann, 2005; Giménez-Fernández et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2013), non-spatial visual features such as color (Addleman & Störmer, 2023; Conn et al., 2020; Sha et al., 2017), or particular real-world objects (Addleman, et al., 2024).

This experiment tests whether incidentally learned pitch regularities facilitate attentional selection and whether such learning persists once statistical regularities are removed.

Sample size was determined based on a pilot experiment (N = 29) that used an identical task but without the thresholding procedure, which yielded an effect size of d ≈ 0.30.

We considered effect sizes in the range of d = 0.20-0.50 to be theoretically meaningful for this paradigm and anticipated that equating perceived loudness across sounds via the thresholding procedure would increase the effect size toward a medium effect (d ≈ 0.50), which requires N = 34 to achieve 80% power (α = 0.05) in a paired t-test.
Accordingly, we aimed to collect approximately 34 participants for Experiments 1 and 2.
Data was collected from 34 participants (mean age = 19 yrs; SD = 1.33; 23 female, 11 male).

For the first four subjects, there were technical issues with the loudspeakers during the first block of the experiment; thus, to avoid losing data, we added an additional learning block for these participants during data collection.

Participants performed an auditory selection task in which two sounds were presented simultaneously from two separate loudspeakers.

text.text: Our goal was to match the sample size of 33 participants from Experiment 1.
To achieve this, we collected data from overall 37 participants between the ages of 18 and 23 years old (mean age = 19.5 yrs; SD = 1.26; 26 female, 11 male).
Individuals provided informed consent before the experiment and were compensated for their participation with course credit or cash ($15/1 hour), following the methods of Experiment 1.
Data from three subjects were excluded from the final analyses because their overall accuracy fell below the apriori determined 75% threshold.
Data from an additional subject was excluded from the analyses because they only completed 18 blocks in the experiment and reported having trouble detecting the gap during the experiment.
Thus, data from 33 participants were retained for final analysis.
The experimental procedure was identical to Experiment 1 except for stimulus type and duration.
Three different stimuli were used across the experiment, each 525 ms in duration: a guitar chord, a piano chord, and a trumpet chord, all created using GarageBand (Apple Inc.).

We increased the stimulus duration by 100ms to provide more time to process the more complex stimulus, since differences in timbre (not low-level features) needed to be processed to make the stimuli discriminable.
All stimuli were composed in C-major (~250 Hz), and instruments were chosen based on general knowledge/familiarity of instrument characteristics.
Participants also completed a post-experiment questionnaire and results are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Statistical analysis procedures were identical to Experiment 1.
Where Mauchly's test for sphericity was violated, identical adjustment procedures to Experiment 1 were conducted.

Participants performed accurately overall (M = 93.21, SD = 4.72), and while participants had higher accuracy in valid compared to neutral and invalid trials: valid (M = 94.25, SD = 5.00), neutral (M = 92.02, SD = 5.62) and invalid (M = 92.60, SD = 6.69), the within-subject ANOVA (GG-correction = 0.64) did not show a significant main effect of trialType (F(1.27, 40.67) = 3.09, p = .08).

There was no significant main effect of Phase (F(0.64, 20.33) = 2.81, p = .12; difference = 0.88, SE = 0.53, p = .10), but a significant interaction effect between trialType & Phase (F(1.27, 40.67) = 4.70, p =.03).

text.text: To again check for repetition priming effects, we followed the analysis strategy of Experiment 1 and removed repetition trials.
One subject fell below the accuracy threshold in this follow-up analysis, so data from 32 participants were used.

With this procedure (GG-correction = 0.33), there was not a main effect for trialType on RT (F(0.66, 20.47) = 4.17, p = .07) and the numerical differences between valid trials vs. invalid trials (difference = 47.92, SE = 22.30, p = .10) and valid vs. neutral trials (difference = 39.98, SE = 19.88, p = .13) was statistically not significant.
Neutral trials were not significantly faster than invalid trials (difference = 7.94, SE = 7.55, p = .98).

While the main effect of Phase remained significant (F(0.33,10.23) = 36.69, p = .001) with faster RTs in the testing phase compared to the learning phase (difference = 67.08, SE = 11.07, p = 1e-6), there was no interaction effect of trialType and Phase (F(0.66, 20.47) = 2.95, p = .11).
These results suggest that at least part of the RT benefits observed for instruments were potentially due to short-term repetition priming.

The present study investigated whether learning about statistical regularities of auditory characteristics (pitch and timbre) improves attentional selection.

Our results demonstrate that people can incidentally learn to prioritize the most relevant feature for both simple and more complex sounds, suggesting that learned attention operates at multiple stages of the auditory processing hierarchy.

Overall, our findings extend prior work demonstrating selection history effects for auditory location (Addleman & Jiang, 2019) and voice category (Daly & Pitt, 2023), as well as different visual features (Addleman & Störmer, 2023; Conn et al., 2020; Geng & Behrmann, 2005; Jiang et al., 2013; Sha et al., 2017; Addleman et al., 2019; Addleman, et al., 2024), suggesting incidental learning of statistical regularities is a general principle of attentional selection across domains.

text.text: While we found significant learning effects for both pitch and instrument chords, we also observed important differences.

First, our results from the feature repetition-priming analysis suggest that pitchbased learning reflects genuine long-term statistical learning and not only short-term effects of priming, whereas instrument-based learning may be -at least in part -attributable to short-term repetition priming.

Thus, at least for more complex auditory objects, short-term priming may play an important role in scaffolding the acquisition of learned selection biases, functioning as a signal that helps orient to true regularities and distinguish them from coincidences (Daly & Pitt, 2023).
text.formatted: Thus, at least for more complex auditory objects, short-term priming may play an important role in scaffolding the acquisition of learned selection biases, functioning as a signal that helps orient to true regularities and distinguish them from coincidences <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Daly & Pitt, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, and consistent with the repetition priming results, the validity effect persisted into the testing phase for learned pitches but was not statistically significant for learned instrument chords.

Notably, the effect sizes were comparable across experiments in both learning (d=0.49 vs. d=0.46) and testing phases (d=0.26 vs. d=0.24), and a post-hoc cross-experiment comparison confirmed no significant difference between them (learning phase: p = 0.87; testing phase: p = 0.86).

The absence of significance in Experiment 2 for the testing phase should therefore not be over-interpreted as evidence of a fundamentally distinct learning mechanism for instrumental timbre vs. pitch; it more likely reflects greater between-person variability or differential influences of feature repetition in the instrument condition.

Yet, it is worth noting that the overall pattern of results are compatible with a multimode view of auditory attention (Johnston & Heinz, 1978), according to which attention can operate flexibly at multiple levels of perceptual analysis, but may differ in its implementation -short-term priming vs. longer-term learning -as well as its effectiveness and durability.

text.text: On this view, the analysis of simple features like pitch occurs relatively automatically, potentially allowing statistical regularities to be tracked and retained with ease, whereas selection on the basis of higher-level features such as timbre engages more complex processing stages, potentially yielding biases that are more context-dependent and less durable.

This interpretation is consistent with Daly and Pitt (2023), who found a strong probability benefit for voice targets in isolation but a substantially reduced effect in more complex situations with nontargets present.

text.text: At a more mechanistic level, it is plausible that the observed differences are due to how the respective acoustic features are represented in the auditory system: pitch is encoded tonotopically from early stages of auditory processing (for review, see Saenz & Langers 2014), providing a stable representational substrate for statistical learning.
text.formatted: At a more mechanistic level, it is plausible that the observed differences are due to how the respective acoustic features are represented in the auditory system: pitch is encoded tonotopically from early stages of auditory processing (for review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Saenz & Langers 2014)</ref>, providing a stable representational substrate for statistical learning.

text.text: Instrument chords, by contrast, require the integration of spectrotemporal information across multiple frequency bands (Bregman 1990; Darwin & Carlyon, 1995; Darwin 1997; Shinn-Cunningham, 2008) -a conjunctive process that may permit learning but render the resulting biases more fragile.

text.text: We emphasize, however, that these interpretations remain tentative given the between-experiment nature of the comparison, and direct confirmation in a within-subjects designwhere pitch and timbre learning are tested in the same participants -is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn.
Future studies could also examine different auditory characteristics, such as rhythm, melody, or real-world (e.g. natural vs. manmade) sounds, to further explore this hypothesis.

Our data also revealed notable variability in the magnitude of the learning effects across specific target sounds, with high-pitch tones (and to a lesser extent the trumpet chord) showing numerically stronger effects (see Fig. 2B and 3B).

text.text: Although we employed a thresholding procedure to equate perceived loudness across sounds, this seemed to not have fully equated perceptual salience across the stimuli.

We acknowledge this as a limitation but also believe it points to a broader and rather underexplored question in the auditory statistical learning literature: stimulus salience and sound identity may meaningfully constrain the magnitude of learning effects.

This may also speak to why effects in Experiment 2 appeared smaller overall, for sounds that are less intrinsically salient (in isolation) or perceptually distinct (when combined in a soundscape) may "steepen the learning curve" of statistical regularities.

Our primary analyses were focused on addressing whether statistical learning occurs at all across auditory features -not to fully characterize how specific stimulus properties modulate it -and future work will be needed to disentangle the contributions of statistical learning and stimulus salience to attentional prioritization in audition.
How might learned auditory attention to pitch and instrument timbre be implemented?

Most models suggest that learning affects attention by modifying weights on priority maps, in which top-down goals, incidental experience, and bottom-up saliency combine to shape what is attended (Awh et al., 2012; Ferrante et al., 2018; Addleman & Jiang, 2019).
text.formatted: Most models suggest that learning affects attention by modifying weights on priority maps, in which top-down goals, incidental experience, and bottom-up saliency combine to shape what is attended <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Awh et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ferrante et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Addleman & Jiang, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Priority map models were originally developed with location as the primary coding scheme, leaving it somewhat unclear how they extend to non-spatial features.

Our findings, alongside work showing robust selection history effects for non-spatial features in the visual domain (Addleman & Störmer, 2023; Ortego et al., 2025; Addleman et al., 2024), suggest that learned attention can operate over non-spatial low-level features as well as more abstract and complex perceptual dimensions.

text.text: The same argument extends to habit-based accounts of attentional learning, which emphasize behavioral routines over detailed probability representations and have likewise been framed primarily in spatial terms (Jiang, 2018 (Jiang, , 2019)).
text.formatted: The same argument extends to habit-based accounts of attentional learning, which emphasize behavioral routines over detailed probability representations and have likewise been framed primarily in spatial terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jiang, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Jiang, , 2019))</ref>.

text.text: Thus, our findings suggest that both priority-map and habit-based mechanisms of attentional learning must be capable of operating at a featurerepresentational level, beyond spatial maps.

The present findings add to a growing literature on experience-dependent attentional prioritization, which includes reward-driven attentional capture, where stimuli associated with differential reward value acquire attentional priority (Anderson, 2016; Asutay & Västfjäll, 2016; Cheng et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The present findings add to a growing literature on experience-dependent attentional prioritization, which includes reward-driven attentional capture, where stimuli associated with differential reward value acquire attentional priority <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Anderson, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Asutay & Västfjäll, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Cheng et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: While it is possible that implicit reward signals contribute to the RT advantages we observe in the present study, we note an important distinction: reward-driven capture paradigms typically involve differential reward contingencies across stimuli, whereas in our paradigm all sounds were associated with identical feedback and thus reward outcomes (i.e., finding the correct target, regardless of pitch/timbre).
The highprobability sound did not yield more reward -it simply occurred as the target more frequently.

Statistical frequency, rather than differential reward value, is therefore the more parsimonious account of the present findings, though both mechanisms may rely on overlapping reinforcement signals at the neural level.
Overall, our results demonstrate that the auditory attentional system can be attuned to a variety of attributes through incidental experience.

The acquisition and durability of such learning may be constrained by the format of the perceptual representations, with higher-level, complex features potentially proving less durable than simple unidimensional ones, and possibly also relying more heavily on short-term priming rather than long-term statistical learning.
Thus, past experience, in conjunction with bottom-up salience and top-down goals, emerges as an important force shaping which sounds we come to prioritize in everyday listening.
